procedural_history.originating_court: Advisory Committee/Jail Advisory Board, then State Government
procedural_history.impugned_order: The State Government's rejection on 01.09.2022 of the Advisory Board's recommendation to release the petitioner.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Not mentioned in the provided text.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner, aggrieved by the State Government's rejection, filed a Writ Petition (Criminal) No. 520 of 2022 in the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the writ petition, seemingly overturning the rejection, based on the fact that the police report did not recommend release. The text also mentions previous considerations and rejections of the petitioner's case by the Advisory Board and State Government.

directions: The writ petition, thus, stands allowed in the above terms.
Pending applications, if any, are disposed of.

issue.issue_text: Whether the writ petition ﬁ led by the petitioner seeking appropriate direction to the State Government, to prematurely release him, having been in custody-actual imprisonment for over 26 years, and served a sentence of over 35 years including over 8 years of remission earned, for oﬀ ence punishable u/ss. 302 and 392 IPC, should be allowed.

facts: The petitioner was convicted for murder (Sec 302 IPC) and robbery (Sec 392 IPC) for a crime committed in 1996 and was serving a life sentence.
He had undergone over 26 years of actual imprisonment and served a total sentence of over 35 years, which included more than 8 years of remission earned for good conduct.
A diverse Jail Advisory Board, after considering all factors, unanimously recommended the petitioner's premature release on three separate occasions (in 2017, 2020, and 2022).
The State Government rejected these recommendations all three times without providing any specific reasons for its decision.
The petitioner's record in prison was positive, as evidenced by the significant remission he earned and the Board's description of him as hardworking, disciplined, and reformed.
law: The court considered various prison rules (both the 1958 and 2014 versions) which allow for the consideration of premature release after a convict has served a certain period (e.g., 14 or 20 years).
Remission is granted to prisoners for keeping peace and good behavior in jail, serving as an indicator of their conduct.
application: The Court found that the petitioner had served a period of incarceration far exceeding the minimums required by any applicable remission policy.
The Court viewed the State Government's repeated rejection of the Advisory Board's unanimous recommendations, without assigning any reasons, as "patently unsustainable."
The petitioner's good conduct was demonstrated by the over 8 years of remission he had earned and the positive reports from the Jail Advisory Board.

The Court concluded that forcing the petitioner to go through the same consideration process again would be "cruel," given his long incarceration, good behavior, and the state's history of arbitrary rejections.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that, in the interest of justice, it was appropriate to directly order the petitioner's release. It found the State Government's repeated and unexplained rejections of the Advisory Board's recommendations to be unsustainable. Given the petitioner's extremely long period of incarceration and demonstrated good conduct, the Court allowed the writ petition and directed his immediate release.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the writ petition ﬁ led by the petitioner seeking appropriate direction to the State Government, to prematurely release him, having been in custody-actual imprisonment for over 26 years, and served a sentence of over 35 years including over 8 years of remission earned, for oﬀ ence punishable u/ss. 302 and 392 IPC, should be allowed.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner, who is 67 years old, was found to be hardworking, disciplined, and reformed by the Jail Advisory Board, which supported his premature release.

The petitioner's counsel relied on several judgments, including State of Haryana v. Jagdish, Maru Ram, v. Union of India, General Oﬃcer Commanding-in-Chief v. Subhash Chandra Yadav, State of Haryana v. Mahender Singh, and State v. H. Nilofer Nisha.
respondent_arguments: The petitioner's case for premature release had been considered 9 times and was repeatedly rejected, with the case being deferred for detailed reports from probation and police officers.
The grant of remission is solely at the executive's discretion and an act of mercy, not an indefeasible right.
A convict only has a right to be considered for remission, which had already occurred in this case.
The decision of whether to grant remission falls exclusively within the domain of the executive.

The State's counsel relied on judgments including Ramdas Athawale v. Union of India, Union of India v. V. Sriharan, State of Haryana v. Mahender Singh, Swamy Shraddananda (2) @ Mural Manohar Mishra v. State of Karnataka, State of Madhya Pradesh v. Ratan Singh, and Rajan v. The Home Secretary, Home Department of Tamil Nadu.

cases.case_name: U.P. State Road Transport Corporation & Anr v. Mohd. Ismail & Ors.
cases.principle: Statutory discretion cannot be fettered by self-created rules or policy, and an authority cannot deny itself the discretion which the statute requires it to exercise in individual cases.

cases.case_name: Chairman, All India Railway Rec. Board & Ors. v. K. Shyam Kumar & Ors.
cases.principle: To explain the issue of administrative discretion.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Statutory discretion cannot be fettered by self-created rules or policy. While an authority may establish norms to regulate the exercise of its discretion, it cannot use those rules to deny itself the discretion that a statute requires it to exercise in individual cases. Guidelines that do not have a statutory basis are merely advisory and cannot have the force of a statute.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the State government's executive policy, which imposed a blanket exclusion on granting premature release to prisoners convicted of certain offenses (like the murder of a woman), was arbitrary and illegal. This policy improperly fettered the statutory discretion that must be exercised on a case-by-case basis, and it contradicted the foundational principles of reformation and rehabilitation that are central to the criminal justice system.
legal_tests_applied: The principle of administrative law that statutory discretion cannot be fettered by self-created rules or policy.

The ground of judicial review for "illegality," which occurs when a decision-maker fails to correctly understand and apply the law that regulates their power, including by fettering their own discretion or acting based on irrelevant factors.
The principle that while an authority can create guidelines for exercising discretion, it cannot deny itself the discretion that the statute requires it to exercise in individual cases.
why_appellant_lost: The State's reliance on an executive policy to create a blanket exclusion of certain offenses from the scope of remission was deemed arbitrary and an illegal fettering of discretion.
The government's policy directive was found to undermine the statutory Act and Rules that govern remission, which cannot be countenanced.
The State's refusal to release the petitioner was based on this flawed policy rather than an individualized assessment of his case, constituting an 'illegality' subject to judicial review.
why_respondent_won: The petitioner had demonstrated good conduct, with the Jail Advisory Board finding him to be hardworking, disciplined, and a reformed inmate, which supported his case for release.
The State's repeated rejection of the petitioner's release was based on an unlawful policy, not on the merits of his individual case, justifying the court's intervention to direct his release.
policy_considerations: The penological goals of reformation and rehabilitation are the cornerstone of the criminal justice system, rather than retribution.
Blanket exclusion policies for remission turn the ideals of reformation that run through the criminal justice system on their head.
